paras: The police shooting at Henry Armistead took place on the evening of December 4, 1880, on Harrison street in Chicago, when two officers fired at a young Black man accused of snatching a watch from a jewelry store. Neither shot hit him, and he was arrested and jailed; the Chicago Daily Tribune reported the episode the next morning as one item in its roundup of petty crime.

According to the Tribune, Armistead entered the jewelry store of H. Benjamin & Brother, No. 88 Harrison street near State, at about 9:30 p.m., "suddenly grabbed a watch," and left through the window. Running across the street, he collided with Officer Con Murphy so hard that both men fell. Armistead got up and ran on, but was "brought up standing" by two pistol shots that the paper attributed to Officers Gillard and Murphy, without saying which officer fired which shot. Neither shot took effect, and the two officers arrested him and locked him up in the Armory.

The Tribune said the affair caused "considerable excitement in the vicinity," but it named no witnesses and gave no account from Armistead. No report of a charge, trial or sentence against Armistead, or of any inquiry into the officers' use of their pistols, was found in the coverage.

The only account located is the Tribune's, printed on page six under the heading "PETTY CRIME" among items on cigar thieves, a shoplifter and a gang of burglars. Alone among the people in that roundup, Armistead was identified by race, as "a young colored thief," and the paper wrote that he had made "a desperate attempt" and "came very near losing his life." The item presented the officers' shooting as the natural end of a chase and offered no comment on it; no wire version, reprint or editorial appeared in other papers searched.

accounts.label: Chicago Daily Tribune police roundup
accounts.gist: Armistead grabbed a watch, fled through the window, collided with Officer Murphy, got up and ran, and was stopped by two shots from Officers Gillard and Murphy, neither of which hit him; he was locked up in the Armory.

framing.detail: The Tribune ran the incident as a routine item under 'PETTY CRIME', labeling Armistead a 'colored thief' and treating the shooting as an incident of the arrest without comment on the officers.

Officers Gillard and Con Murphy of the Chicago police

sources.note: Only account: 'Petty Crime' roundup item on the watch grab at 88 Harrison street, two officers' shots that missed, and the arrest.
quotes: A young colored thief named Henry Armistead made a desperate attempt to get away with a watch last evening, and came very near losing his life.
Armistead got up and run away, but was brought up standing by two pistol-shots fired by Officers Gillard and Murphy, who arrested him and locked him up in the Armory.
Neither of the shots took effect. The affair caused considerable excitement in the vicinity.
